title: Did a Monk Discover Halley's Comet 600 Years Before Halley?
summary: Have you ever seen a shooting star and made a wish? Now imagine seeing a giant, glowing comet with a long tail — and then seeing the exact same one again, decades later! That's what a monk named Eilmer of Malmesbury did almost 1,000 years ago. New research says he may have been the first person to figure out that comets can come back, long before the famous astronomer Edmond Halley. Halley's Comet is one of the most famous comets ever. It zooms past Earth about every 76 years. In 1066, it blazed across the sky and was seen all over the world — even in China for over two months! People back then thought comets were bad omens, warning of war or the death of a king. In fact, that same year, King Harold of England died in the Battle of Hastings, and the comet was stitched into the famous Bayeux Tapestry. Eilmer was an old monk when he saw the comet in 1066. He remembered seeing it before, way back in 989, and he realized it was the same one returning. A historian named William of Malmesbury wrote about this, but nobody paid much attention until now. Researchers Simon Portegies Zwart and a historian named Lewis dug into the old texts and found that Eilmer's story was the real deal. So, should we still call it Halley's Comet? The researchers think maybe not, since Eilmer figured out the pattern centuries earlier. Portegies Zwart said the research was "great fun" but also tricky because he had to work with a historian. They plan to study more old comet sightings. Next time you hear about Halley's Comet (it'll be back in 2061!), remember the monk who may have spotted its secret first.
why_it_matters: This story shows that even a monk a thousand years ago could make an important discovery, reminding you that great observations can come from anyone and old tales can still surprise us.

background_read: Halley's Comet has been recorded for over 2,000 years, appearing every 75–76 years.
The Bayeux Tapestry (a huge embroidered cloth from the 11th century) shows the comet and King Harold to mark the Norman Conquest.
Edmond Halley (an English astronomer) realized in 1705 that several past comets were the same one returning, and he correctly predicted its next visit.
Article_Structure: WHO: A monk named Eilmer of Malmesbury, and modern researchers Simon Portegies Zwart and a historian named Lewis.
WHAT: New research suggests Eilmer was the first to understand that comets can return, long before Edmond Halley.
WHERE: The comet was seen from England; the research was based on old texts from Malmesbury Abbey.
WHY: Historians and astronomers now believe Eilmer's account is credible, which could change how we remember the discovery of Halley's Comet.

perspectives.description: Eilmer's insight proves that ancient observers were very smart, and their records can still teach us new things about the sky.
Some historians think Eilmer only saw two bright comets and didn't prove they were the same, so the comet should remain named after Halley, who used math to predict its return.
The research is part of a bigger effort to learn from historical sky observations, which helps us understand how comets have appeared and been understood over time.
